name: The Baldwin Effect
statement: What a species first learns to do, it may over generations be born able to do.
statementAccent: over generations be born able to do
meaning: The Baldwin effect proposes that a learned or plastic behaviour that improves fitness can, over generations, become genetically encoded and instinctive — through ordinary natural selection, without any Lamarckian inheritance of acquired traits. Learning and plasticity keep a lineage alive in new conditions long enough for genetic variants that produce the trait innately, more reliably or cheaply, to arise and be favoured. What is inherited is not the learned behaviour but a heightened capacity to develop it.
mechanism: When organisms meet a new environment, those able to learn or flex their phenotype survive where rigid ones would fail. That survival changes the selective landscape: now genotypes that generate the adaptive trait with less learning, more reliably, or at lower cost enjoy higher fitness. Over generations, selection canalises the trait, so it comes to be produced with less environmental input and can become largely innate. Learning thus guides evolution by reshaping which genotypes are favoured, never by writing acquired states back into the genome.

examples.text: Hinton and Nowlan's 1987 simulation showed that organisms able to learn evolved much faster toward a set of co-adapted genes than non-learners, even though nothing learned was passed to the genome — the canonical modern demonstration.

Waddington's fruit-fly experiments, heat-shocking pupae to produce a crossveinless wing and selecting over generations, eventually fixed the trait so it appeared without the shock — a related, experimentally demonstrated mechanism.
A behaviour first acquired by learning in a new niche can, if consistently adaptive, become increasingly innate across generations as selection favours the readiest learners and then the born-ready.

variants.name: Genetic assimilation
variants.text: Waddington's related but distinct mechanism, in which an environmentally induced phenotype becomes canalised and eventually appears without the inducing cue — often confused with the Baldwin effect but not identical.

variants.name: Organic selection
variants.text: Baldwin's own term for the idea, proposed independently and near-simultaneously in 1896 by Lloyd Morgan and Osborn, before George Gaylord Simpson named it the Baldwin effect in 1953.

whyItMatters: It offers a Darwinian way for learning and behavioural flexibility to influence the course of genetic evolution, a bridge between what organisms do in their lifetimes and what their descendants inherit. Consistent with the modern synthesis yet reaching toward the extended evolutionary synthesis and niche construction, it remains a touchstone in debates over how plasticity shapes evolution.

working.text: treat plasticity and learning as changing the selective environment, which can steer genetic evolution toward innate versions of adaptive traits.
remember that nothing acquired is inherited; only heritable variation in the capacity to develop the trait is selected.
separate the Baldwin effect from Waddington's genetic assimilation, a related mechanism that should not be conflated with it.

limits: The effect is theoretically accepted and consistent with Darwinism, but its real-world importance is genuinely contested. The most compelling demonstrations remain computational models and laboratory genetic-assimilation experiments rather than unambiguous cases in nature. Mayr objected that its classical framing focuses on individual genotypes rather than populations and underweights that plasticity is itself genetically controlled. Some argue it is nothing more than standard selection acting on plasticity, and that the speeding-up seen in models can be a computational illusion. Its prevalence and force in real evolution stay debated.
misreadings: The Baldwin effect is not Lamarckian — it involves no inheritance of acquired characteristics, only ordinary selection on genetic variation, with learning changing the selective environment. The learned behaviour itself does not become heritable; only the capacity or propensity to develop it does. And model-based speed-ups of evolution do not prove the effect is a major force in nature, a claim that remains disputed.
origin: Proposed by the psychologist James Mark Baldwin in 'A New Factor in Evolution' (American Naturalist, 1896), and independently by Conwy Lloyd Morgan and Henry Fairfield Osborn under the name organic selection; George Gaylord Simpson named it the Baldwin effect in 1953, and Waddington's genetic assimilation gave a related experimental mechanism.

sources.text: Baldwin effect, Wikipedia. — the statement, the 1896 origins, Simpson's naming, and the relation to genetic assimilation.
Hinton & Nowlan, "How Learning Can Guide Evolution," Complex Systems 1(3):495-502 (1987). — the model showing learning accelerates evolution without inheriting the learned trait.
Genetic assimilation, Wikipedia. — Waddington's crossveinless and bithorax experiments as a related demonstrated mechanism.
